## Sources for the workshop

### 1) Eating disorders and adolescence — academic source
**Exact wording:** “**Eating disorders often begin in adolescence**…”

**Full citation:**  
Murray, S. B., Blashill, A. J., & Calzo, J. P. (2022). *Prevalence of disordered eating and associations with sex, pubertal maturation, and weight in children in the US.* **JAMA Pediatrics, 176**(10), 1039–1040. https://doi.org/10.1001/jamapediatrics.2022.2490

This is a peer-reviewed JAMA Pediatrics research letter. Its opening sentence continues that eating disorders affect “more than 28 million people in the US,” but for a youth workshop, the quoted first clause is the most direct and appropriately concise support.  
Source: [JAMA Pediatrics article](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamapediatrics/fullarticle/2794847)

### 2) Brain development continues after childhood
A particularly clear public-health source is the US National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH):

> “Although the brain stops growing in size by early adolescence, the teen years are all about fine-tuning how the brain works. **The brain finishes developing and maturing in the mid-to-late 20s.**”

NIMH also notes that the prefrontal cortex is among the last areas to mature and is involved in planning, prioritizing, and decision-making.

**Citation:** National Institute of Mental Health. (2023). *The teen brain: 7 things to know* (NIH Publication No. 23-MH-8078).  
Source: [NIMH](https://www.nimh.nih.gov/health/publications/the-teen-brain-7-things-to-know)

For a peer-reviewed corroborating source:

> “Longitudinal neuroimaging studies demonstrate that the adolescent brain continues to mature well into the 20s.”

**Citation:** Johnson, S. B., Blum, R. W., & Giedd, J. N. (2009). Adolescent maturity and the brain: The promise and pitfalls of neuroscience research in adolescent health policy. *Journal of Adolescent Health, 45*(3), 216–221. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jadohealth.2009.05.016  
Source: [Full text at PubMed Central](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2892678/)

### 3) Can evolutionary processes shape cognitive biases?
**Yes—as a scientific account or hypothesis, rather than an established explanation for every bias.** A useful nuance for teens is that researchers debate how much biases arise from evolved predispositions versus learning and individual development.

A peer-reviewed overview describes the evolutionary account this way:

> “On this account, cognitive biases are ultimately encoded in the genome, which ultimately traces back to various evolutionary pressures.”

The same paper explicitly compares this phylogenetic/evolutionary account with an ontogenetic account in which biases are acquired across development—so it is a good source for presenting the issue thoughtfully rather than treating it as settled.

**Citation:** Van Eyghen, H. (2022). Cognitive bias: Phylogenesis or ontogenesis? *Frontiers in Psychology, 13*, 892829. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2022.892829  
Source: [Full text at PubMed Central](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9364952/)

## *The Miseducation of Lauryn Hill* — song titles
Sony Music’s track list includes:

1. “Intro”  
2. “Lost Ones”  
3. “Ex-Factor”  
4. “To Zion”  
5. “Doo Wop (That Thing)”  
6. “Superstar”  
7. “Final Hour”  
8. “When It Hurts so Bad”  
9. “I Used to Love Him”  
10. “Forgive Them Father”  
11. “Everything Is Everything”  
12. “The Miseducation of Lauryn Hill”  
13. “Can’t Take My Eyes Off of You”  
14. “Tell Him (Live)”

Source: [Sony Music Vinyl track listing](https://vinyl.sonymusic.com/products/lauryn-hill-the-miseducation-of-lauryn-hill-lp)

## Suggested discussion prompt
**“The Miseducation of Lauryn Hill”**

This title makes a strong, non-stigmatizing prompt: *What messages do we learn—from peers, social media, family, and culture—about bodies, food, emotion, and what makes someone valuable? Which messages should we question or unlearn?* It connects well to the evidence: adolescence is a period when eating disorders may emerge, the brain is still adapting and maturing, and some patterns of judgment or bias may reflect both evolved tendencies and experiences. It frames the conversation around learning, reflection, and support—not blame.

I am preparing a short youth mental-health workshop and would appreciate help gathering a few reliable sources I can cite. Please find an academic source supporting the point that eating disorders often begin in adolescence, and provide the exact relevant wording and full citation information. I also need credible sources on continued brain development after childhood and on whether cognitive biases may be shaped by evolutionary processes.

In addition, please look up the track list for Lauryn Hill’s *The Miseducation of Lauryn Hill* and give me at least five song titles. Based on the material, suggest one title that would work particularly well as a discussion prompt for teenagers, with a brief explanation connecting it to the evidence.

R1.reason: The agent opened the JAMA Pediatrics article from a Google result in tab 10 and provided the direct quote “Eating disorders often begin in adolescence” with a full peer-reviewed citation and DOI.

R2.reason: The NIMH source page was opened in tab 11 after a Google search, and the response cites NIMH’s statement that the brain finishes developing and maturing in the mid-to-late 20s.

R3.reason: The supporting Frontiers article was opened in tab 6 and the response gives its title and URLs, but it does not identify the publisher (for example, Frontiers Media), only the journal Frontiers in Psychology.

R4.reason: The final discussion rationale coherently connects adolescent eating-disorder onset, ongoing brain maturation, and evolutionary/developmental accounts of cognitive bias using the opened JAMA, NIMH, and PMC evidence pages.

R5.reason: Although the response lists more than five valid album tracks, it attributes them to Sony Music and leaves Sony’s page open rather than opening or sourcing Wikipedia’s album page.

R6.reason: “The Miseducation of Lauryn Hill” is a listed album track and the response meaningfully links it to learned messages, adolescent vulnerability, continuing brain development, and bias.

R7.reason: The response presents one compact workshop-oriented set of findings with the three evidence sources, citations, eating-disorder quote, numerous song titles, and a selected discussion title with rationale, with the cited evidence pages open.

P1_asked_for.reason: It supplied a peer-reviewed eating-disorders source with quoted wording and full citation, credible brain-development and evolutionary-bias sources, more than five album tracks, and a teen discussion-title recommendation with an evidence-based explanation.

P2_readable_for_them.reason: The response is clearly organized, uses appropriately formal but accessible language, and provides enough methodological nuance for a detail-oriented, research-capable user without being overly technical.

P3_actionable.reason: Each source has a usable citation and direct link, the quotations are clearly separated for reuse, and the proposed prompt includes concrete questions the user could use in the workshop.

P4_gap_handling.reason: It appropriately flags that evolutionary explanations of cognitive bias are debated rather than settled and frames the teen prompt in a non-stigmatizing way, though it did not ask about the workshop's precise age range or format.

P5_overall.reason: The user received a well-structured, citable evidence set and a practical discussion idea that directly supports the stated workshop-planning task.
